entry: [[Pakistan|Pakistani]] singer, songwriter and master of qawwali, a Sufi devotional music of Pakistan and India. Trained in classical khayal under his father and uncles, he became head of the family qawwali party in 1971 and is credited with introducing qawwali to international audiences. He was known for performances lasting several hours and for his vocal intensity. He recorded film scores and albums in Europe, India, Japan, Pakistan and the United States, and collaborated with Western artists, among them [[Peter Gabriel]]. [[Jeff Buckley]] called him "my Elvis." [[Rolling Stone]] ranked him among its 200 greatest singers of all time, and [[The New York Times]] called him the greatest qawwali singer of his generation. He performed in over 40 countries and recorded more than 125 albums.

Fruit with a hard shell enclosing a single seed. In botany, a nut is indehiscent, meaning its shell does not open to release the seed. Most seeds come from fruit that frees them, but true nuts, such as [[Hazelnut|hazelnuts]], [[Chestnut|chestnuts]] and acorns, have hard shell walls and develop from a compound ovary, so they rely on animals, such as herbivores that eat and excrete them, for seed dispersal. True nuts come from plant families of the order Fagales, including beech, oak and hazel. Walnuts and hickories, including [[Pecan|pecans]], are considered nuts under some definitions. Nuts used for food are a common source of food allergens, which can be life-threatening, and tree nut allergy is distinct from [[Peanut|peanut]] allergy, though experts suggest that people allergic to peanuts avoid tree nuts, and vice versa. Nuts supply many calories from unsaturated fats and are rich in B vitamins, vitamin E and essential amino acids.

Type of [[Fastener|fastener]] with a threaded hole that mates with a bolt. Nuts are almost always used with a bolt to fasten parts together, held by thread [[Friction|friction]], slight elastic deformation and compression. Where vibration could loosen them, lock washers, jam nuts or thread-locking fluid may be used. The square nut was the first shape made, but the [[Hexagon|hexagonal]] nut is most common today, because six sides give a tool good angles of approach and corners are less likely to round off. Wing nuts allow adjustment by hand. Nuts and bolts were once handmade as matched pairs; Joseph Whitworth proposed a standard in 1841. The Crystal Palace, built for the Great Exhibition of 1851, used standardized sizes, and the Whitworth standard was widely adopted afterward. A British standard was not formally adopted until 1905.

Spice made from the seed of the evergreen tree *Myristica fragrans*. Ground nutmeg flavors baked goods, puddings, meats, sauces and beverages such as [[Eggnog|eggnog]], while mace, from the seed's reddish covering, is more delicate. The tree is native to the Banda Islands in Maluku, [[Indonesia]], which are the main producing area, and Indonesia supplies over 75% of the global market. Nutmeg has been used in folk medicine for its psychoactive properties, but its supposed [[Aphrodisiac|aphrodisiac]] effects lack clinical support. High doses can cause acute [[Psychosis|psychosis]], with greater risk during [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]]. In 1621 the [[Dutch East India Company]] took control of the Banda Islands to enforce a monopoly on the trade.

Herbivorous semi-aquatic [[Rodent|rodent]] native to South America. Known as the coypu in South America and Britain, *Myocastor coypus* lives in burrows along waterways and feeds on aquatic and riparian vegetation. Adults typically weigh 4–9 kg (9–20 lb) and have webbed hind feet, a white muzzle patch and large orange-yellow incisors. Introduced mainly by fur farmers to North America, Europe and Asia, it is considered [[Invasive species|invasive]] in several countries, where it damages [[Wetland|wetland]] vegetation and infrastructure through feeding and burrowing. It is still hunted for its fur in some regions. Some populations can carry pathogenic *Leptospira*, though the epidemiological significance is scarce and region-specific. The name nutria, from the Spanish word for otter, is used in North America and Asia.

Capital and most populous city of [[Greenland]], an autonomous territory of Denmark (pop., 2025: 20,113). Founded in 1728 as the colony of Godthaab, it lies at the end of the Nuup Kangerlua [[Fjord|fjord]] on the [[Labrador Sea]]. Its latitude makes it the world's northernmost capital, a few kilometers north of [[Reykjavík]]. Nuuk is the Greenlandic word for "cape." Since home rule in 1979, Greenlandic names have been preferred, and Nuuk replaced Godthaab. A [[Smallpox|smallpox]] epidemic in 1733 and 1734 killed most of the native population.

American multinational technology company headquartered in Santa Clara, California. Founded in 1993 by [[Jensen Huang]], Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, it began with [[Graphics processing unit|graphics processing units]] (GPUs) for gaming. It now makes GPUs, systems on chips and application programming interfaces for data science, high-performance computing, [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] and automotive applications. In 2025 it became the first company to surpass US$4 trillion and then US$5 trillion in market capitalization, driven largely by the [[AI boom|AI boom]] and demand for its AI data center hardware.

Family of synthetic [[Polymer|polymers]] characterized by [[Amide|amide]] linkages. Nylons are thermoplastics that can be melt-processed into fibers, films and molded shapes. [[DuPont]] began its nylon research in 1927, building on its experience with [[Rayon|rayon]]. Chemist Wallace Hume Carothers synthesized the first nylon, nylon 66, on February 28, 1935. DuPont announced nylon in 1938 and obtained a patent for the polymer that year. Some varieties have a [[Silk|silk]]-like appearance. During [[World War II]], nylon was used in [[Parachute|parachutes]] and tires. Today nylons are used for apparel, carpeting, rubber reinforcement, automotive and electrical parts, and food packaging films.

Juvenile form of some [[Invertebrate|invertebrates]], especially [[Insect|insects]], resembling the adult without wings. Unlike a [[Larva|larva]], a nymph already has the adult's form, apart from lacking wings and not yet having developed genitalia. It undergoes gradual metamorphosis without a [[Pupa|pupal]] stage, and its final molt produces the adult. Many insect orders have nymphs, including Orthoptera, Hemiptera, mayflies, termites, cockroaches, mantises and dragonflies, as do arachnids such as [[Spider|spiders]], mites and ticks. Aquatic nymphs are called naiads. In 1628 English physician [[William Harvey]] hypothesized that pupal forms came from imperfect eggs, an outdated idea that still contributed to understanding nymphs. Nymph imitations account for over half of the fly-fishing patterns regularly used in the United States.

Minor female nature deity in ancient [[Greek mythology|Greek]] folklore. Nymphs were typically tied to a specific place, landform or tree and depicted as maidens. Because of their association with springs, they were often seen as having healing powers. Their other divine powers included [[Divination|divination]] and shapeshifting, and though divine, they were not immortal. Subgroups included the Dryads of [[Oak|oak]] trees, the Naiads of springs and the Nereids of the sea. Often attendants of goddesses such as [[Artemis]], they appear in myths of love with heroes and deities. Since the [[Middle Ages]], they have sometimes been confused with fairies.

Ambundu queen of Ndongo and Matamba in present-day northern [[Angola]]. Born into Ndongo's ruling family, she was trained in military and political affairs and served as an ambassador to the [[Portuguese Empire]]. She took power in 1624, during rapid growth of the slave trade and Portuguese encroachment. After Portugal declared war in 1626 she went into exile, conquered Matamba from 1631 to 1635, and in 1641 allied with the Dutch West India Company, reclaiming much of Ndongo. Portugal retook [[Luanda]] in 1648, and a peace treaty was signed in 1656. Late in life she promoted Catholicism and aligned closely with Portugal, which granted her a monopoly of slave exports in exchange for trade and a military alliance. She is remembered for her diplomacy and [[Military tactics|military tactics]].

Intergovernmental economic organization of 38 member countries, founded in 1961. It was created to stimulate economic progress and world trade, and its members describe themselves as committed to democracy and the market economy. The OECD is headquartered at the Château de la Muette in [[Paris]] and funded by member contributions. It succeeded the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation, which had distributed American aid for reconstruction after [[World War II]]. Japan joined in 1964. As of 2026 its members had a combined population of 1.38 billion and produced 58.4% of global nominal GDP. The OECD publishes annual economic reports, evaluations and rankings. Critics argue that it has shifted from growth-oriented policy toward regulatory harmonization that burdens smaller economies.

Third studio album by the English rock band [[Radiohead]]. Released May 21, 1997, it was recorded with producer Nigel Godrich in Oxfordshire and at St Catherine's Court in Bath. Its abstract lyrics depict a dystopian world of consumerism, social alienation and technological anxiety. It reached number one on the UK Albums Chart and sold at least 7.8 million copies worldwide. Its singles included "Paranoid Android" and "Karma Police." It won the [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Award]] for Best Alternative Music Album in 1998, and in 2014 the [[Library of Congress]] added it to the National Recording Registry.

Type of [[Light-emitting diode|light-emitting diode]] whose emissive layer is a film of [[Organic compound|organic compound]]. Each pixel emits its own light and needs no backlight, an advantage over [[Liquid-crystal display|liquid-crystal displays]]. OLEDs are used in [[Smartphone|smartphones]], [[Computer monitor|computer monitors]] and televisions. Active-matrix displays (AMOLED) use a thin-film transistor to switch each pixel, allowing higher resolution. Chemists Ching Wan Tang and Steven Van Slyke of Eastman Kodak are credited with the invention in 1987. Commercial use began in 1997 with a Pioneer car stereo.

Intergovernmental cartel of oil-producing and oil-dependent countries. Founded in 1960 in [[Baghdad]] by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela, it aims to let members collectively influence the global oil market and maximize profit. Its members accounted for 38 percent of global oil production in 2022 and are estimated to hold 79.5 percent of proven oil reserves. Economists describe it as a textbook example of a cartel. Political scientist Jeff Colgan has argued that since the 1980s it has largely failed to achieve its goals, with members cheating on 96 percent of their commitments between 1982 and 2009. OPEC+, formed in 2016 with other producers, extends the group's coordination. The [[United Arab Emirates]] left OPEC and OPEC+ in 2026.

[[American football|American football]] running back and actor. He won the 1968 Heisman Trophy for the USC Trojans and in 1973 became the first player in the [[National Football League|National Football League]] to rush for more than 2,000 yards in a season. He later acted in the *Naked Gun* films. A 1995 criminal trial acquitted him of the 1994 murders of his former wife Nicole Brown and Ron Goldman, but a 1997 civil case found him liable for the murders. In 2008 he was convicted of armed robbery and [[Kidnapping|kidnapping]] in [[Las Vegas]].

Hardwood tree or shrub of the genus *Quercus* in the [[Beech|beech]] family. Oaks are widely distributed across the Northern Hemisphere, with some 475 species, both deciduous and evergreen. Each acorn is a [[Nut (fruit)|nut]] borne in a cup. Oaks are keystone species that support more than 950 species of caterpillar and form associations with fungi, including [[Truffle|truffles]]. Their leaves and acorns contain enough [[Tannin|tannin]] to be toxic to cattle. Oak timber is strong and hard, used in construction and [[Furniture|furniture]] making, and oak [[Wine|wine]] barrels age sherry and [[Whisky|whisky]]. Almost a third of oak species are threatened with extinction from [[Climate change|climate change]], pests and habitat loss. The oak is a symbol of strength and the national tree of many countries.

City in the East Bay region of the [[San Francisco Bay Area|San Francisco Bay Area]] in [[California]] (pop., 2020: 440,646), seat of Alameda County. Incorporated in 1852 during the California gold rush, it became the western terminus of the Transcontinental Railroad in 1869. The Port of Oakland is the busiest port in Northern California. Many San Francisco residents moved to Oakland after the 1906 earthquake, and the Bay Bridge linked the two cities in 1936. Oakland was also the birthplace of the [[Black Panther Party]] in 1966.

Pelagic lampriform fish of the family Regalecidae, comprising three species. The giant oarfish (*Regalecus glesne*) is the longest bony fish alive, reaching about 8 m (26 ft). Oarfish have silvery, scaleless bodies, a long crest-like dorsal fin and no swim bladder. They often self-amputate the tail, and their gelatinous flesh is not well regarded for eating. Because they are rarely seen and sometimes linger at the surface when sick or dying, they are a probable source of historical sea serpent tales. Their beachings before storms gave them a reputation as harbingers of doom, a folk belief reinforced by the numerous beachings before the [[2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami|disastrous 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami]]. Oarfish feed on [[Krill|krill]], [[Squid|squid]] and other small animals.

Fertile area of a [[Desert|desert]] or semi-desert that sustains plant life and provides habitat for animals. Oases depend on water from springs, underground rivers or [[Aquifer|aquifers]], accessed by natural flow or by human-made wells and channels, and most are artificial. Oases in West Asia and [[North Africa]] cover about 1,000,000 hectares (10,000 km²) yet support about 10 million inhabitants. Archaeological evidence of settlement at Ein Gedi in the Dead Sea Valley dates to 6,000 BC. Oases were stops on caravan routes, and control of an oasis often meant control of the trade along a route.

English rock band formed in [[Manchester]] in 1991. Its core members were brothers Liam and Noel Gallagher. Both *Definitely Maybe* (1994) and *(What's the Story) Morning Glory?* (1995) reached number one in Britain, the latter spending ten weeks there amid a chart rivalry with [[Blur (band)|Blur]]. The band played two nights at Knebworth in 1996 for about 125,000 people each night. It disbanded in 2009 and reunited in 2024. As of 2026 the band has sold over 100 million records, and it was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]].

[[Cereal|Cereal]] grass (*Avena sativa*) grown for its seeds and as fodder. Oats appear to have been domesticated as a secondary crop, because their seeds resembled those of other cereals closely enough for early cultivators to include them. They tolerate cold winters less well than [[Wheat|wheat]], [[Barley|barley]] and [[Rye|rye]], but need less summer heat and more rain, which makes them important in cool, wet regions such as Northwest Europe. Oats tolerate low-nutrient and acid soils and compete well with weeds. One of the most common uses is [[Livestock|livestock]] feed, but oats are also eaten as oatmeal, including steel cut and rolled oats. Canada and Russia dominate production. Regular consumption is associated with lower blood [[Cholesterol|cholesterol]] and reduced risk of heart disease.

State in southern [[Mexico]] with a [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific]] coastline. Its capital is Oaxaca de Juárez. The state is best known for its [[Indigenous peoples|Indigenous peoples]], mainly the Zapotecs and Mixtecs, and 16 groups are officially recognized. Most live in the Central Valleys, home to the archaeological site of Monte Albán, a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]]. Oaxaca is one of Mexico's most biologically diverse states, ranking in the top three for reptiles, amphibians, mammals and plants. Of its 570 municipalities, 418 are governed by *usos y costumbres* (customs and traditions).

Major river in western [[Siberia]], Russia. With its tributary the Irtysh, it forms the world's seventh-longest river system, at 5,410 kilometers (3,360 mi). It forms at the confluence of the Biya and Katun rivers, which rise in the [[Altai Mountains]], and flows northwest, then north, into the Gulf of Ob, the world's longest [[Estuary|estuary]] and an arm of the [[Kara Sea]]. The main city on its banks is [[Novosibirsk]], Siberia's largest city, where the [[Trans-Siberian Railway]] crosses the river. The Ob provides irrigation, drinking water, hydroelectric power and fishing. It is icebound at southern Barnaul from early November to near the end of April.

[[Programming paradigm]] based on objects, software entities that encapsulate data and functions. A program in this paradigm consists of objects that interact with one another. The idea of objects emerged in the artificial intelligence group at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in the late 1950s and early 1960s, and Simula, developed in Norway from 1961 to 1967, introduced classes, inheritance and dynamic binding. Alan Kay developed Smalltalk at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, and object-oriented programming rose to prominence in the 1980s. Principles often cited are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism. Languages such as [[C++]], [[Java (programming language)|Java]], [[Python (programming language)|Python]] and [[JavaScript]] support it, though classifying a language as object-oriented is debatable.
